title: Binary Number with Alternating Bits
notes:
Task and constraints: Check whether every adjacent pair of bits in positive integer `n` differs.
Idea: `hasAlternatingBits` saves the low bit in `prev`, shifts right, and compares each next low bit with the preceding bit.
Technique and why it applies: Binary right shifts expose bits from least significant to most significant, so one comparison per adjacent pair is enough.
Invariant: `prev` stores the last examined bit, and all adjacent pairs already examined differ if the method has not returned false.
Edge cases: A one-bit number returns true; the input is assumed positive; any equal adjacent bits cause immediate failure.
Complexity: The loop processes O(log n) bits and uses O(1) auxiliary space.
complexity_reason: Each right shift exposes the next bit, and the previous-bit variable detects equal neighbors.

title: Binary Number with Alternating Bits
notes:
Task and constraints: Determine whether the binary representation of positive `n` alternates between zero and one.
Idea: `hasAlternatingBits` captures `n & 1`, shifts `n`, then compares each subsequent low bit to `prev`.
Technique and why it applies: Shifting right traverses the representation one bit at a time without converting it to a string.
Invariant: Every pair of bits processed so far differs unless the method has returned false.
Edge cases: Single-bit values return true; the method assumes a positive input; one repeated adjacent bit is enough to reject.
Complexity: Processing each binary digit takes O(log n) time and O(1) auxiliary space.
code: class Solution { public boolean hasAlternatingBits(int n){int prev=n&1;n>>=1;while(n>0){int bit=n&1;if(bit==prev)return false;prev=bit;n>>=1;}return true;} }
complexity_reason: The loop runs once per remaining binary digit and stores only the previous bit.

title: Max Area of Island
notes:
Task and constraints: Find the largest four-directionally connected component of land cells (`1`) in a binary grid.
Idea: `maxAreaOfIsland` scans every cell and starts an explicit-stack DFS for each unseen land cell, marking cells in `seen` and counting `area`.
Technique and why it applies: Flood fill visits exactly one connected island at a time; a visited set prevents repeated counting and stack overflow from recursive DFS.
Invariant: Each land cell is marked before it is pushed, so every cell contributes to at most one component area.
Edge cases: Empty grid returns zero; water cells are skipped; only horizontal and vertical neighbors count as connected.
Complexity: Each cell and its four neighbors are checked a constant number of times, giving O(mn) time and O(mn) auxiliary space.
complexity_reason: Marking cells when pushed prevents duplicate stack entries and counts every island cell exactly once.

title: Max Area of Island
notes:
Task and constraints: Return the maximum area of a land island connected by up, down, left, and right neighbors.
Idea: `maxAreaOfIsland` scans the matrix and uses an `ArrayDeque<int[]>` DFS with `seen` to count each component.
Technique and why it applies: Iterative flood fill discovers all cells reachable from a starting land cell, while a boolean matrix records visits efficiently.
Invariant: Every cell pushed onto `st` is land and already marked seen, so no cell is counted twice.
Edge cases: Empty outer grid returns zero; diagonal land cells do not connect; water and previously visited cells are ignored.
Complexity: All m-by-n cells are examined with constant neighbor work, yielding O(mn) time and O(mn) space.
code: class Solution { public int maxAreaOfIsland(int[][] grid){if(grid.length==0)return 0;int m=grid.length,n=grid[0].length,best=0;boolean[][]seen=new boolean[m][n];int[]dr={1,-1,0,0},dc={0,0,1,-1};for(int r=0;r<m;r++)for(int c=0;c<n;c++)if(grid[r][c]==1&&!seen[r][c]){ArrayDeque<int[]>st=new ArrayDeque<>();st.push(new int[]{r,c});seen[r][c]=true;int area=0;while(!st.isEmpty()){int[]v=st.pop();area++;for(int k=0;k<4;k++){int x=v[0]+dr[k],y=v[1]+dc[k];if(x>=0&&x<m&&y>=0&&y<n&&grid[x][y]==1&&!seen[x][y]){seen[x][y]=true;st.push(new int[]{x,y});}}}best=Math.max(best,area);}return best;} }
complexity_reason: The boolean visit matrix and four direction offsets enforce unique, orthogonal island traversal.

title: Count Binary Substrings
notes:
Task and constraints: Count substrings with equal counts of consecutive zeroes and ones, with each character grouped contiguously.
Idea: `countBinarySubstrings` tracks the previous group length `prev` and current group length `cur`, adding `min(prev,cur)` at each group boundary and once at the end.
Technique and why it applies: Every valid substring crosses exactly one boundary between adjacent runs, and the shorter run limits how many equal-sized pairs can be formed.
Invariant: `ans` contains contributions from all completed adjacent run pairs; `prev` and `cur` describe the last two runs.
Edge cases: Empty string returns zero; a single run contributes zero; finalizing after the loop counts the last pair.
Complexity: One pass gives O(n) time and O(1) auxiliary space.
complexity_reason: Each boundary between runs contributes the smaller run length, and the final pair is added after scanning.

title: Count Binary Substrings
notes:
Task and constraints: Count binary substrings with equal numbers of zeroes and ones where each side is one consecutive group.
Idea: `countBinarySubstrings` counts the current run in `cur`; on a character change it adds `Math.min(prev,cur)`, shifts run lengths, and finally adds the remaining pair contribution.
Technique and why it applies: Valid substrings are formed across neighboring runs, with their number limited by the shorter run.
Invariant: `prev` and `cur` are the lengths of the previous and current runs, and `ans` sums finalized boundaries.
Edge cases: Empty input returns zero; all identical bits produce zero; the final boundary must be counted after the loop.
Complexity: The loop visits each character once, so time is O(n) and auxiliary space is O(1).
code: class Solution { public int countBinarySubstrings(String s){int prev=0,cur=1,ans=0;for(int i=1;i<s.length();i++){if(s.charAt(i)==s.charAt(i-1))cur++;else{ans+=Math.min(prev,cur);prev=cur;cur=1;}}return ans+Math.min(prev,cur);} }
complexity_reason: The shorter of two neighboring run lengths determines how many balanced substrings cross their boundary.

title: Degree of an Array
notes:
Task and constraints: Find the shortest contiguous subarray whose degree equals the maximum frequency of the full array.
Idea: `findShortestSubArray` builds `count`, `first`, and `last` maps, finds the maximum frequency, and minimizes `last[x]-first[x]+1` over values with that frequency.
Technique and why it applies: For any value attaining the array degree, its shortest covering subarray spans from its first occurrence to its last occurrence.
Invariant: After scanning, the maps hold each value's frequency and extremal indices, sufficient to evaluate all degree-attaining candidates.
Edge cases: A non-empty array is assumed because `max(count.values())` fails on empty input; a unique most frequent value is handled by the same minimization.
Complexity: The scan and candidate pass are O(n) expected time with O(n) map storage.
complexity_reason: First and last occurrences give the shortest interval containing every occurrence of a degree-attaining value.

title: Degree of an Array
notes:
Task and constraints: Return the minimum subarray length among values whose frequency equals the whole array's degree.
Idea: `findShortestSubArray` builds count, first-index, and last-index maps, then checks `last-first+1` for every value with maximum frequency.
Technique and why it applies: A candidate interval must include the first and last occurrence of its value, and that interval is sufficient to contain all occurrences.
Invariant: The three maps describe every distinct value's count and occurrence span after the first pass.
Edge cases: Input is assumed non-empty because `Collections.max` needs a value; multiple values can share the degree and compete for shortest span.
Complexity: Two passes over the array and hash maps take O(n) expected time and O(n) space.
code:
import java.util.*;
class Solution { public int findShortestSubArray(int[] nums){Map<Integer,Integer>count=new HashMap<>(),first=new HashMap<>(),last=new HashMap<>();for(int i=0;i<nums.length;i++){int x=nums[i];count.put(x,count.getOrDefault(x,0)+1);first.putIfAbsent(x,i);last.put(x,i);}int degree=Collections.max(count.values()),best=nums.length;for(int x:count.keySet())if(count.get(x)==degree)best=Math.min(best,last.get(x)-first.get(x)+1);return best;} }
complexity_reason: The second pass compares spans only for values whose count matches the computed degree.

title: Search in a Binary Search Tree
notes:
Task and constraints: Return the subtree rooted at the node equal to `val`, or `None` if it is absent.
Idea: `searchBST` iteratively compares `val` with `root.val`, following left when smaller and right when larger until a match or null.
Technique and why it applies: The BST ordering property discards half of the remaining search direction at each visited node.
Invariant: If the target exists, it must be in the subtree currently referenced by `root`.
Edge cases: Empty root returns `None`; missing values eventually reach null; the returned node includes its entire subtree rather than only the value.
Complexity: Time is O(h) for tree height and auxiliary space is O(1).
complexity_reason: BST ordering chooses exactly one child at each step, avoiding traversal of unrelated subtrees.

title: Search in a Binary Search Tree
notes:
Task and constraints: Find and return the BST subtree rooted at the target value, or null if no node matches.
Idea: `searchBST` loops while root exists and differs from `val`, selecting `root.left` or `root.right` from the comparison.
Technique and why it applies: BST ordering means all smaller values lie left and all larger values lie right, so only one path needs inspection.
Invariant: The target, if present, remains within the subtree referenced by `root` on every iteration.
Edge cases: Null root and absent target return null; a successful result is the original matching subtree root.
Complexity: The search takes O(h) time and O(1) auxiliary space.
code: class Solution { public TreeNode searchBST(TreeNode root,int val){while(root!=null&&root.val!=val)root=val<root.val?root.left:root.right;return root;} }
complexity_reason: The iterative loop follows one root-to-leaf path and does not allocate recursion frames.

title: Insert into a Binary Search Tree
approach_name: Insert at the first null child
notes:
Task and constraints: Insert `val` into a BST and return the original root, preserving BST order.
Idea: `insertIntoBST` creates a `TreeNode` at a null position, otherwise recursively inserts left for smaller values and right for values not smaller.
Technique and why it applies: BST comparisons identify the unique insertion path; linking the returned child reconnects the modified subtree to its parent.
Invariant: Every recursive call returns a BST containing the original subtree values plus `val` when inserted below it.
Edge cases: An empty tree creates the root; equal values follow the right branch in this implementation; recursion depth depends on tree shape.
Complexity: Search and insertion take O(h) time and O(h) recursion space.
complexity_reason: The null-child base case inserts exactly once, and recursive returns reconnect the changed branch.

title: Insert into a Binary Search Tree
approach_name: Insert at the first null child
notes:
Task and constraints: Add `val` to the BST and return its root while retaining the BST property.
Idea: `insertIntoBST` returns a new node at null, recurses left when `val < root.val`, and otherwise recurses right.
Technique and why it applies: Ordered comparisons choose the insertion branch, and assigning the recursive result to the child pointer preserves the existing tree.
Invariant: Each returned subtree remains a BST and contains the inserted value exactly once.
Edge cases: Null input creates a new root; equal values go right; a skewed tree can cause linear recursion depth.
Complexity: O(h) time follows the search path and O(h) stack space is used.
code: class Solution { public TreeNode insertIntoBST(TreeNode root,int val){if(root==null)return new TreeNode(val);if(val<root.val)root.left=insertIntoBST(root.left,val);else root.right=insertIntoBST(root.right,val);return root;} }
complexity_reason: Only one branch is visited, and the returned child reference is attached at each ancestor.

title: Binary Search
notes:
Task and constraints: Return the index of `target` in a sorted array, or `-1` when it is absent.
Idea: `search` maintains inclusive bounds `lo` and `hi`, checks midpoint `mid`, and discards the half that cannot contain the target.
Technique and why it applies: Sorted order guarantees the target lies left of a midpoint smaller than it, or right of a midpoint larger than it.
Invariant: If present, the target remains within the inclusive interval `[lo,hi]`.
Edge cases: Empty input skips the loop and returns `-1`; target at either endpoint is handled; duplicates may return any matching index.
Complexity: Halving the interval each iteration gives O(log n) time and O(1) auxiliary space.
complexity_reason: Each comparison eliminates about half of the remaining sorted interval.

title: Binary Search
notes:
Task and constraints: Find the index of a target in sorted `nums`, returning `-1` if absent.
Idea: `search` loops over inclusive `lo` and `hi`, computes overflow-safer `mid = lo + (hi-lo)/2`, then updates one bound.
Technique and why it applies: Binary search uses sorted ordering to discard the half that cannot contain the target after each comparison.
Invariant: Every possible target index remains inside `[lo,hi]` until found or the interval becomes empty.
Edge cases: Empty arrays return `-1`; endpoints are included; duplicates do not guarantee the first matching index.
Complexity: The search interval halves each iteration for O(log n) time and O(1) auxiliary space.
code: class Solution { public int search(int[] nums,int target){int lo=0,hi=nums.length-1;while(lo<=hi){int mid=lo+(hi-lo)/2;if(nums[mid]==target)return mid;if(nums[mid]<target)lo=mid+1;else hi=mid-1;}return -1;} }
complexity_reason: The midpoint formula avoids adding both bounds directly, and each iteration halves the candidate range.

title: To Lower Case
notes:
Task and constraints: Convert an ASCII string to lowercase and return the resulting string.
Idea: `toLowerCase` delegates the full conversion to Python's `s.lower()` method.
Technique and why it applies: The built-in string operation handles character-wise case conversion and constructs the resulting immutable string.
Invariant: The output preserves character order and differs only by lowercase conversion rules.
Edge cases: Empty input returns an empty string; already lowercase input remains unchanged; the problem assumes ASCII semantics.
Complexity: Conversion takes O(n) time and O(n) output space.
code:
class Solution:
 def toLowerCase(self,s):return s.lower()
complexity_reason: The built-in lowercase operation scans the input and returns a new string.

title: To Lower Case
notes:
Task and constraints: Convert the given ASCII string to lowercase.
Idea: `toLowerCase` returns `s.toLowerCase(Locale.ROOT)` to avoid dependence on the machine's default locale.
Technique and why it applies: Locale-independent casing makes ASCII conversion stable across environments with different default language settings.
Invariant: Character order is preserved while uppercase letters are converted to lowercase.
Edge cases: Empty input returns empty; already lowercase text is unchanged; `Locale.ROOT` prevents locale-specific casing behavior.
Complexity: The conversion takes O(n) time and O(n) space for the returned string.
code: class Solution { public String toLowerCase(String s){return s.toLowerCase(Locale.ROOT);} }
complexity_reason: Using `Locale.ROOT` makes lowercase conversion deterministic instead of relying on the host locale.

title: 1-bit and 2-bit Characters
approach_name: Parse bits from left to right
notes:
Task and constraints: Determine whether the final character in the bit array is a one-bit `0`, given `0` as one-bit and `10`/`11` as two-bit encodings.
Idea: `isOneBitCharacter` advances `i` by `bits[i]+1` until it reaches or passes the last position, then checks equality with the final index.
Technique and why it applies: A leading zero consumes one bit and a leading one consumes two, so greedy parsing follows valid character boundaries.
Invariant: `i` always points to the start of the next encoded character.
Edge cases: The input is assumed to end with zero; a final index reached exactly means the last zero starts a one-bit character.
Complexity: Each parsed character advances the index by one or two, giving O(n) time and O(1) space.
complexity_reason: The index jumps by the encoding length, so it never interprets a two-bit character's second bit as a start.

title: 1-bit and 2-bit Characters
approach_name: Parse bits from left to right
notes:
Task and constraints: Return true when the last encoded character is one bit long under the given 0/10/11 encoding.
Idea: `isOneBitCharacter` advances index `i` by `bits[i]+1` while before the last position, then checks whether `i` equals the final index.
Technique and why it applies: Reading the first bit determines whether the next character consumes one or two bits, allowing a left-to-right parse.
Invariant: `i` always identifies a character start, never a continuation bit.
Edge cases: Valid input ends in zero; empty arrays are outside the usual constraints; arriving at the final index means that zero is a one-bit character.
Complexity: At most O(n) bits are consumed and auxiliary space is O(1).
code: class Solution { public boolean isOneBitCharacter(int[] bits){int i=0;while(i<bits.length-1)i+=bits[i]+1;return i==bits.length-1;} }
complexity_reason: The loop stops before parsing the final bit separately, leaving the equality test to classify it.

title: Find Pivot Index
notes:
Task and constraints: Find an index where the sum strictly to its left equals the sum strictly to its right, or return `-1`.
Idea: `pivotIndex` computes `total`, tracks `left`, and checks `left == total-left-x` before adding the current value.
Technique and why it applies: Subtracting the current value and left sum from total gives the right sum without building prefix or suffix arrays.
Invariant: Before testing index `i`, `left` equals the sum of elements before `i`.
Edge cases: Empty input returns `-1`; first and last indices are valid candidates with one side sum zero; negative values also work.
Complexity: Computing total and scanning are O(n) time, with O(1) auxiliary space.
complexity_reason: Subtracting the current value and left sum from the total yields the right-side sum in constant time.

title: Find Pivot Index
notes:
Task and constraints: Return a pivot index whose left and right element sums are equal, or `-1` if no pivot exists.
Idea: `pivotIndex` first sums all values, then scans while maintaining `left` and checks `left == total-left-nums[i]`.
Technique and why it applies: The total sum lets the method derive the right sum in constant time for each candidate index.
Invariant: At the start of each iteration, `left` is the sum of all entries before `i`.
Edge cases: Empty arrays return `-1`; endpoints can qualify; the algorithm works with negative numbers as well as positive numbers.
Complexity: Two linear passes give O(n) time and O(1) auxiliary space.
code: class Solution { public int pivotIndex(int[] nums){int total=0;for(int x:nums)total+=x;int left=0;for(int i=0;i<nums.length;i++){if(left==total-left-nums[i])return i;left+=nums[i];}return -1;} }
complexity_reason: The running left sum and overall total avoid allocating additional prefix and suffix arrays.
